newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey pressures Cyprus to scrap missile deal.
newsitem.headline: Turkey pressures Cyprus to scrap missile deal.

text.p: Turkey on Friday again threatened military action against Cyprus to stop it deploying Russian missiles and said it might occupy an abandoned tourist resort on the island if the Cypriot government did not back down.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said Turkey could knock out an anti-aircraft missile system the Greek Cypriot government plans to install under a deal made with Russia last weekend.
"These offensive missiles will definitely not be deployed. If they are deployed we will do what is needed, if that means they need to be hit they will be hit," Ciller told reporters.

The Cypriot government, which insists the S-300 missiles are defensive, dismissed the warnings and said it would concentrate on a political solution, adding that the missiles would not be delivered for at least 16 months anyway.

Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash added to the war of words in Nicosia with a statement warning of moves to integrate the abandoned "ghost resort" of Varosha into the Turkish sector of the island if the rocket plan was not scrapped.

Varosha -- once the island's top tourist resort and mostly owned by Greek Cypriots -- has been left abandoned but still under Turkish military control since 1974 when Turkey invaded Cyprus after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
Turkey has some 30,000 troops in the northern third of Cyprus which declared itself a Turkish Cypriot state but is only recognised by Ankara.
The internationally recognised Greek Cypriot government in the south of the divided island commands a national guard of over 10,000 troops and is backed militarily by Athens.
Cypriot ministers have dismissed Turkey's tough talk, but Cyprus stocks plunged 1.75 percent over the week on concern about the missile dispute.

"Every day we are hearing one or two new threats. We are not going to follow the line of Turkey. We are going to concentrate on a political solution to the Cyprus problem," Cypriot Foreign Minister Alecos Michaelides told Reuters.
Ciller accused NATO ally Greece of encouraging the Cypriot government to create a missile crisis in the Mediterranean.
"Greece is undoubtedly the country which holds most responsibility for this aggressive policy and which is encouraging, directing and supporting (Cyprus) on this path."
NATO allies Ankara and Athens almost came to blows a year ago in a row over ownership of a deserted islet in the Aegean Sea.
The United States and Britain have urged Cyprus to cancel the Russian missile deal and Washington is to send an envoy to the island over the weekend to try to reduce the tension.
Cyprus confirmed U.S. estimates that the system will not be deployed for at least 16 months. "That is not inaccurate," Michaelides said. "There is at least that much time."
The United Nations, which patrols a buffer zone between the island's two communities, said it opposed any attempt to change the status of Varosha.
